'''Timothy M. Caro''' (born 1951) is a British [[evolutionary ecology|evolutionary ecologist]] known for his work on [[conservation biology]], [[Ethology|animal behaviour]], [[anti-predator defence]]s in animals, and the function of zebra stripes. He is the author of several textbooks on these subjects.

==Life==

Caro was born in 1951 to artists [[Anthony Caro]] and [[Sheila Girling]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kerlin |first=Kat |date=14 December 2016 |title=Biologist earns his 'Zebra Stripes' with new book |url=https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/biologist-earns-his-zebra-stripes-new-book |access-date=2022-05-23 |website=University of California |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lynton |first=Norbert |date=24 October 2013 |title=Sir Anthony Caro obituary |url=http://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2013/oct/24/sir-anthony-caro |access-date=2022-05-23 |website=[[The Guardian]] |language=en}}</ref> Caro gained his bachelor's degree in [[zoology]] at [[Cambridge University]] in 1973, and his doctorate in psychology at the [[University of St Andrews]] in 1979. He was a professor of wildlife biology at [[University of California, Davis]], in the departments of population biology and wildlife and fish conservation biology. He is currently a professor of biology at the [[University of Bristol]]. He has studied the colour [[Polymorphism (biology)|polymorphism]] of [[coconut crab]]s, the [[conservation (ethic)|conservation]] of fragments of forest, and the function of [[animal coloration|coloration in mammals]], especially zebra stripes.<ref name="UCDavis">{{cite web|title=Tim Caro|url=http://wfcb.ucdavis.edu/people/faculty/caro-tim/|publisher=University of California Davis|access-date=8 January 2018}}</ref><ref name="Profile">{{cite web|title=Tim Caro Profile|url=http://biosci3.ucdavis.edu/Faculty/Profile/View/14114|publisher=University of California Davis|access-date=8 January 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Dr. Tim Caro: Unraveling the Mysteries of Animal Coloration and Why Zebras Have Stripes|url=http://www.peoplebehindthescience.com/dr-tim-caro/|website=People Behind the Science Podcast|access-date=8 January 2018|date=7 June 2014}}</ref>

===How the zebra got its stripes===
[[File:Three Zebras Drinking.jpg|thumb|Caro investigated some 18 hypotheses to explain why zebras are striped, excluding all but one of them through experimental studies.]]

Caro's team found evidence that zebra stripes help to reduce biting by [[Horse-fly|tabanid]] flies, but no reliable support for traditionally held hypotheses about the function of zebra stripes including [[camouflage]], [[predator avoidance]], heat management, or social interaction.<ref name="CaroIzzo2014">{{cite journal |last1=Caro |first1=Tim |last2=Izzo |first2=Amanda |last3=Reiner |first3=Robert C. |last4=Walker |first4=Hannah |last5=Stankowich |first5=Theodore |title=The function of zebra stripes |journal=Nature Communications |volume=5 |year=2014 |doi=10.1038/ncomms4535 |pmid=24691390 |bibcode=2014NatCo...5.3535C |page=3535|doi-access=free |hdl=1983/a698e989-4948-4e53-80c8-bb01520f3f3a |hdl-access=free }}</ref> He evaluated 18 different proposed explanations for the stripes, devising and carrying out quantitative tests to compare them. The evolutionary ecologist Tim Birkhead, writing in the ''Times Higher Education'', praised Caro's 2006 book ''Zebra Stripes'' as "an exemplary study", calling it "one long argument", a phrase used by [[Charles Darwin|Darwin]] of his ''[[On the Origin of Species]]'', summarising it as "in essence a 300-page scientific paper".<ref name="THE">{{cite news |last1=Birkhead |first1=Tim |title=Zebra Stripes, by Tim Caro |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/books/review-zebra-stripes-tim-caro-university-of-chicago-press |work=[[Times Higher Education]] |date=8 December 2016}}</ref> Karin Brulliard, writing in ''[[The Washington Post]]'' under the headline "To figure out why the zebra got its stripes, this researcher dressed up like one", portrays Caro in a zebra costume "not used in his fieldwork", but also in a tailor-made striped suit in the Tanzanian bush, as well as in pelts of zebra and the unstriped wildebeest. The newspaper reports Caro as "absolutely convinced" that he has found the right explanation.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brulliard |first1=Karin |title=To figure out why the zebra got its stripes, this researcher dressed up like one |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/animalia/wp/2017/01/04/to-figure-out-why-the-zebra-got-its-stripes-this-researcher-dressed-up-like-one/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=4 January 2017}}</ref> [[Matthew Cobb]], writing in ''[[New Scientist]]'', recalls [[Rudyard Kipling]]'s children's book, ''[[Just So Stories]]'', in which the zebra got his stripes by standing half-in, half-out of the shadows "with the slippery-slidy shadows of the trees" on his body. Cobb calls ''Zebra Stripes'' a marvellous book and predicts it will encourage a generation to "tackle evolutionary biology's remaining enigmas, with or without the help of Kipling."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cobb |first1=Matthew |author-link= Matthew Cobb| title=How did the zebra get its stripes? |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg23331170-600-how-did-the-zebra-get-its-stripes/ |work=[[New Scientist]]}}</ref>
Michael Lemonick, writing in ''[[The New Yorker]]'' echoed the just-so-story theme.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Lemonick |first1=Michael |title=How Zebras Got Their Stripes |url=https://www.newyorker.com/tech/elements/how-zebras-got-their-stripes |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=11 April 2014}}</ref>
